content: The return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) refers to the restoration of sustained, effective cardiac activity that is accompanied by significant respiratory effort following cardiac arrest. Clinical indicators of ROSC include the presence of breathing, coughing, or physical movement, as well as a palpable pulse or measurable blood pressure. The likelihood of achieving ROSC is significantly increased through the use of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation. The phenomenon known as the Lazarus phenomenon, or autoresuscitation, describes the spontaneous return of circulation after resuscitation efforts have been discontinued in a patient who experienced cardiac arrest. For this reason, it is recommended to continue passive monitoring for at least 10 minutes after resuscitation attempts have ceased. Hyperthermia, or fever, is observed in approximately 42% of patients following cardiac arrest and is associated with worse neurological outcomes and a poor overall prognosis. As part of post-cardiac arrest care, induced therapeutic hypothermia is often employed to mitigate these effects. The underlying pathophysiology of fever in this context is thought to be driven by an early systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Cardiac arrest results in ischemia and subsequent reperfusion injury throughout the body, which triggers an inflammatory cascade. Patients who survive cardiac arrest frequently exhibit elevated levels of cytokines, dysregulated cytokine production, and increased plasma endotoxins. These immunological abnormalities closely resemble the pathophysiological changes observed in sepsis.
